source.titleEnglish: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
source.objectiveEnglish: Recognize jobsite cognates and use survival phrases when you do not understand.
source.focusSpanish: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad and -ente, plus survival phrases for getting help
source.speakingEnglish: Tell a coworker you speak a little Spanish, ask them to speak more slowly, and ask what a jobsite word means.
source.readerTitleSpanish: Palabras y ayuda en la obra

archivedDraft.title: Morning check-in review
archivedDraft.scene: Sato checks the carpenters and materials with Tanaka, asks about the saw Tanaka is holding, and confirms tomorrow's gathering at the work site
materialDrift: Archived Japanese Foundation 10 reviews Sato and Tanaka's morning check-in, carpenter count, tools, and next-day meeting. Current Spanish source teaches cognates and help requests through Tom and Luis at a Houston construction site, inspection, electricity, concrete pouring, and 911. These scenes and saved positions are distinct.

cards.sourceNoteInternal: -ción words are feminine and match English -tion.
-dad words are feminine and match English -ty.

cards.japaneseDraft: すみません、分かりません。

cards.sourceEnglish: Can you speak more slowly, please?
cards.japaneseDraft: もう少しゆっくり話していただけますか。

cards.sourceEnglish: I need help with the installation.

reader.sourceSpanish: Tom es capataz en una construcción en Houston.
reader.sourceEnglish: Tom is a foreman at a construction site in Houston.
reader.japaneseDraft: トムはヒューストンの建設現場で職長をしています。

reader.sourceSpanish: Tom le dice a Luis: Hablo un poco de español.
reader.sourceEnglish: Tom tells Luis: I speak a little Spanish.

reader.sourceSpanish: Luis dice: El cliente pide una inspección urgente hoy.
reader.sourceEnglish: Luis says: The client asks for an urgent inspection today.

reader.sourceSpanish: Tom: ¿Puede hablar más despacio, por favor?
reader.sourceEnglish: Tom: Can you speak more slowly, please?
reader.japaneseDraft: トム：「もう少しゆっくり話していただけますか。」

reader.sourceSpanish: Tom oye una palabra y pregunta: ¿Qué significa colar?
reader.sourceEnglish: Tom hears a word and asks: What does colar mean?

reader.sourceSpanish: Luis explica: Colar es echar el concreto en la forma.
reader.sourceEnglish: Luis explains: Colar means to pour the concrete into the form.

reader.sourceSpanish: Luis dice: Primero revisamos la calidad de la instalación eléctrica.
reader.sourceEnglish: Luis says: First we check the quality of the electrical installation.

reader.sourceSpanish: Tom le dice al equipo: Por seguridad, apaguen la electricidad primero.
reader.sourceEnglish: Tom tells the crew: For safety, turn off the electricity first.

reader.sourceSpanish: Tom dice: En una emergencia o un accidente, llamen al 911.
reader.sourceEnglish: Tom says: In an emergency or an accident, call 911.
reader.japaneseDraft: トムは言います。「緊急事態や事故のときは、911に電話してください。」

decisionsNeeded: The objective teaches Spanish cognates ending in -ción, -dad, and -ente and survival phrases for Spanish. Choose a Japanese-specific objective and decide how to retain exact source coverage before selecting cards or Reader turns 2, 5, and 6.

Choose contextual Japanese senses for inspection, client, and installation, including electrical installation and quality of installation; do not assert a single dictionary headword before qualified construction review.

Keep source colar and its explanation, pouring concrete into the form, visible. Decide whether to show the Spanish term as quoted source language or teach a Japanese construction term; do not silently replace the source action.
Resolve the source's Spanish-speaking phrases and its usted/ustedes register against Japanese workplace roles and audience before selecting card 13 or 15, or the Reader equivalents.
Review the instruction to turn off electricity before selecting Reader 8. Preserve its safety meaning without inventing a procedure, authorization, or equipment state.
The scene is in Houston and the source says 911. The US National 911 Program confirms 911 for emergency assistance; qualified locale and domain review still precedes any learner-facing recording.

Map six exact authored mode prompt/target pairs, forms, speaking, dictionary and saved-item identities after qualified text selection. Verify exact text and each recording, then obtain a separate human listening decision for every clip.
